_note: This page restates a number from every page it links to, so every claim here re-runs against THAT PAGE'S OWN shipped data file and then checks the derived file this page renders from against the same recomputation. A correction upstream fails this page's gate instead of leaving a stale tile behind, and a derive script that was not re-run fails it too. The pattern is index/claims.json's; the paths climb out of cluster-health/data/ on purpose.

Both readings appear on the tile and this claim requires each one to carry its basis wherever it is printed.

claims.assert: (lambda ser, s: s['value'] == ser[max(ser)] and s['low']['value'] == min(ser.values()) and s['low']['year'] == 2023 and s['high']['value'] == max(ser.values()) and s['high']['year'] == 2019 and s['rank_from_low'] == 4 and s['n_years'] == len(ser) == 7 and s['better_end'] == 'high' and s['year_prefix'] == 'FY' and 2026 not in ser)({y: round(sum(r['real'] for r in D['fed']['naics'] if r['fy'] == y), 6) for y in sorted(set(r['fy'] for r in D['fed']['naics'])) if y != max(set(r['fy'] for r in D['fed']['naics']))}, D['h']['tiles'][4]['standing'])
claims.falsified_if: FY2026 closing, which adds an eighth year to the rail and changes the rank; the same scheduled event the baseline claim is the alarm for. Also falsified if the open year is ever drawn on this rail, which would put a partial year beside seven full ones.

claims.source: The declared merit direction in derive_health.py, asserted against what the page renders from

claims.text: The broader-industry note compares the same three codes (326, 3252, 3255) over 2022–2025: national private employment fell from 909,558 to 857,188, down 5.8 percent, against PIC-12's 8.0 percent on its fixed disclosed county-industry set. The region fell faster. The rates do not identify a causal share of regional losses.
claims.source: cluster-health/data/tide.json (QCEW US000, fetched 2026-08-30); the regional figures re-run against health.json
claims.assert: (lambda t, R: (lambda u22, u25, r22, r25: u22 == 909558 and u25 == 857188 and round((u25 / u22 - 1)*100,1)==-5.8 and round((r25 / r22 - 1)*100,1)==-8.0 and r25/r22 < u25/u22)(one(x['us_register_emp'] for x in t['trend'] if x['year'] == 2022), one(x['us_register_emp'] for x in t['trend'] if x['year'] == 2025), one(x['balanced'] for x in R if x['year'] == 2022), one(x['balanced'] for x in R if x['year'] == 2025)))(D['tide'], D['h']['register']['disclosed'])
claims.actual: ([x for x in D['h']['register']['disclosed'] if x['year'] in (2022, 2025)], D['tide']['trend'], round((one(x['us_register_emp'] for x in D['tide']['trend'] if x['year'] == 2025) / one(x['us_register_emp'] for x in D['tide']['trend'] if x['year'] == 2022) - 1) / (one(x['balanced'] for x in D['h']['register']['disclosed'] if x['year'] == 2025) / one(x['balanced'] for x in D['h']['register']['disclosed'] if x['year'] == 2022) - 1), 4))
claims.falsified_if: Either series revises the two rates apart, or the region stops falling faster than its industry. Re-based twice. 2026-08-30: a naive reader caught the first version comparing the region's three-industry register to a national series of 326 alone, a one-industry tide under a three-industry fall. 2026-09-01: the window was 2023 to 2025 while the run it explains is 2022 to 2025, and a three-year fall divided by a two-year tide is not a share of anything. On the matched window the industry accounts for 72 percent rather than the 60 the page printed, which moves the reading and not only the arithmetic.
